own_scenes.desc: Neil Rushton, coleccionista de northern soul de Birmingham y dueño de Kool Kat, fue a Chicago a fichar house, oyó hablar de Detroit y desvió el viaje: contactó con May, que le presentó a Saunderson, y licenció «Nude Photo», «The Sound», «Our Music» y «Groovin’ without a Doubt». Como en los viejos recopilatorios de Motown, convenció a Mick Clark de Virgin (sello 10) para juntar Transmat, KMS y Metroplex, con 20.000 libras de presupuesto que nunca se recuperaron, licencias de discos que ni existían, cheques supuestamente falsificados y un lío de samples con Todd Terry. Iba a llamarse The House Sound of Detroit, pero Atkins entregó al final «Techno Music», con voz sintética a lo Computer World, y Rushton cambió el título: así nació el nombre que separó a Detroit del house. Lo que tiró del disco fue «Big Fun», que Saunderson trajo el último día en una caja de cintas (y May hizo «It Is What It Is» esa misma noche): Top 10 británico en otoño de 1988. May aterrizó en Londres como «la cara humana de la música de máquinas», con los de A&R haciendo cola, y Stuart Cosgrove lo llamó en The Face «Seventh City Techno», música «post-soul» que «refuta el pasado». Aun así vendió menos de lo esperado; fracasaron un disco con Herbie Hancock y el supergrupo Intellex de May y Atkins con ZTT, que quería unos «Pet Shop Boys negros» y se echó atrás porque May no iría a Top of the Pops. Techno 2: The Next Generation (1990), con Carl Craig, Octave One y Jay Denham, llegó cuando Londres ya se había cansado: «la moda había pasado».

refs.q: Rushton was instantly prompted to change the compilation’s title to Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit. Just like that, the name for Detroit’s dance music was born, setting it apart from house and defining it as a new musical genre in its own right.
refs.para: One of the last artists to contribute to the compilation was Atkins, who had just returned from an extended trip to California. Atkins turned in a song called “Techno Music,” which used the same integration of speech synthesis Kraftwerk had used throughout its 1981 album Computer World. The voice “sang” out repeated refrains of “I program my home computer” and “techno music.” Rushton was instantly prompted to change the compilation’s title to Techno! The New Dance Sound of Detroit. Just like that, the name for Detroit’s dance music was born, setting it apart from house and defining it as a new musical genre in its own right.
refs.chapter: Cap. 4: Nation to Nation: Finding a Home in Britain’s Rave Culture, 1988–1991

refs.q: People loved Derrick . . . he was a complete star from the moment you met him.”
refs.para: As it turned out, “Big Fun” would be a fortunate choice—it went on to become a Top 10 hit on the U.K. Gallup Top 40 in fall 1988, throwing Saunderson and partner Paris Grey into the wild world of pop stardom. Saunderson, who typifies the reserved and introspective techno producer to a degree, initially seemed uncomfortable with his newfound success. But then, Atkins, May, and Saunderson each had his own way of relating to the hype surrounding the compilation. “Kevin, Juan, and Derrick were such good people to interview in different ways,” Rushton offers. “Kevin being really nice and playing the ‘genial giant,’ even though his music’s dead powerful and represents the way he looks. Juan was so soft-spoken [and] interesting, and Derrick because he’s completely mad. People loved Derrick . . . he was a complete star from the moment you met him.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 4: Nation to Nation: Finding a Home in Britain’s Rave Culture, 1988–1991

refs.q: Nobody’s claiming that we invented electronic music. Some people tend to think of it that way and they get all bent out of shape. Techno is something that just happened.
refs.para: As far as I know, nobody had applied technology to music using that term [“techno”], especially in dance music. You had electronic musicians out there, but most of them were really abstract. Nobody’s claiming that we invented electronic music. Some people tend to think of it that way and they get all bent out of shape. Techno is something that just happened. People looked at you like you have some big, preconceived plan, [but] it’s the general public who designated us to be who we are.
refs.chapter: Cap. 4: Nation to Nation: Finding a Home in Britain’s Rave Culture, 1988–1991

refs.q: We got an anguished call from [ZTT] saying, ‘We can’t do it because Derrick won’t go on Top of the Pops.’
refs.para: Unfortunately, communication between May and Rushton got lost because of some other side issue, and the ZTT deal fell through. Rushton explains: “We got an anguished call from [ZTT] saying, ‘We can’t do it because Derrick won’t go on Top of the Pops.’ I said, ‘Well, that’s OK. That’s part of the allure, isn’t it? You can’t have [an underground artist like] Derrick May on Top of the Pops, can you?’ The whole thing collapsed and I got blamed for that. It was an ultimate contrast in expectations—a U.K. record company trying to be hip.”
refs.chapter: Cap. 4: Nation to Nation: Finding a Home in Britain’s Rave Culture, 1988–1991
